A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RF-HGN research despite the revised title. Their text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A-H are readable and support reliable matching across versions.

before.justification: V1 reports original optimizer comparisons, mass-spring simulations, zero-shot generalization experiments, architecture benchmarks and appendix analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds molecular dynamics simulations, noise experiments, batching evaluations and random Fourier feature comparisons.

M1.justification: Appendix H.5 adds a training variant that solves least-squares problems on subsampled batches and averages the resulting last-layer coefficients. The core invariant encoders, message passing and original SWIM/ELM training equations remain unchanged. B.4's additional sampling implementation details do not establish a revision to the original procedure.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates mass-spring lattices and open and closed chains. V2 adds nonlinear Lennard-Jones molecular systems, including static nine-particle graphs and dynamic-edge generalization from 36 to 64 particles, plus noisy-state evaluation scenarios. The 10,000-node lattice coverage already existed in v1.

E2.justification: Appendix H.6 newly evaluates random Fourier features alongside SWIM and ELM. The optimizer membership in Table 1 and the seven architecture comparators in v1 Table 2, now v2 Table 3, are unchanged.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce molecular trajectory sampling with a 90:10 split, encoder/network widths of 40/800, GELSD solves and long rollout evaluations. Noise and batching experiments introduce five-fold cross-validation with 1,000- and 5,000-state training/test sets, respectively. Existing spring benchmark protocols are retained; the extra description of the existing width ablation is disclosure rather than evidence of rerunning it.

E4.justification: V2 retains the width ablation, convergence comparisons and existing generalization diagnostics. Appendices H.4-H.6 add Gaussian-noise sensitivity tests, direct-versus-batched training analyses measuring accuracy, time and memory, and sensitivity to node/edge and message-encoder RFF scales.

E5.justification: The new noise and batching studies specify five-seed averaging and five-fold cross-validation. V1's three-run mean/minimum/maximum reporting and ten-seed lattice analyses remain unchanged; v2 does not establish additional runs for those retained experiments.

E6.justification: The original optimizer scores, architecture training times and width-ablation values are unchanged. V2 adds substantial molecular, noise, batching and RFF results. For example, its nine-particle evaluation reports final position relative errors of 0.09413 for SWIM and 0.2555 for Adam in Table 2 and Table H.24. These are newly reported results, not improvements over corresponding v1 measurements.

T1.justification: Appendix B.4 adds runtime reasoning for translation encoding, O(MNd), and rotational encoding, O(MNd²). Appendix C adds the molecular Hamiltonian; the existing spring Hamiltonians are merely relocated. No new theorem or proof appears. The added Eq. (C.9) prints an unsquared momentum norm, leaving its intended kinetic term unclear.

C1.justification: V2 narrows the contribution wording from first combining random sampling with graph models to combining it with physics-informed Hamiltonian graph models, and explicitly extends its demonstration claims to molecular systems. The principal rapid-training and 8-to-4096-node zero-shot claims are retained.

C2.justification: V2 adds a tentative explanation of ELM failures through non-isotropic inputs, discusses how tuning can improve data-agnostic features, and explains memory-versus-runtime tradeoffs in batching. Its limitations remove v1's unexplored-dynamic-graph qualification after adding such experiments, but also remove the warning that other graph architectures can be more accurate. The graph-degree generalization boundary remains.

D1.justification: V2 supplies molecular data-generation instructions, model and optimizer settings in Tables D.12-D.15, and an additional hardware entry. It also documents batch coefficient averaging and RFF sampling parameters. B.4 newly discloses SWIM candidate-pair subsampling, while Appendix F identifies the existing ablation's eight-node system and 2,000 training/test samples. The public code address is unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting RFF, LSQR and LSMR, removes several biomedical application citations and the Fang et al. graph-kernel discussion, and narrows its novelty wording to physics-informed graph models. Most related-work positioning is retained. Publication updates and the duplicated LSRN reference do not constitute new research coverage.

P1.justification: The title changes from without gradient descent to using random features. Selected introductory, related-work and conclusion passages are edited, spring Hamiltonians move to Appendix C, and a reproducibility statement is added. Most existing method prose and the main section hierarchy remain closely matched.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document template and table layout, moves Figure 1 onto the first page, and relocates v1 Figure 6 to Figure H.10. Figure 4 gains a molecular-system panel, and new molecular rollout figures and experimental tables substantially expand the displays. Table F.20 corrects v1 Table F.15's swapped encoder/linear-width labels without changing its numerical entries.

improvement.justification: V2 extends empirical support beyond spring systems and makes noise sensitivity, feature tuning and batching tradeoffs more assessable. Corrected ablation labels and added implementation details also help reproducibility. These gains are tempered by inconsistent molecular reporting: Table 2 calls a nine-to-nine-particle evaluation zero-shot, and Eq. (C.9)'s kinetic term is unclear. Removing the qualification about more accurate alternative architectures also weakens the limitations discussion. The net improvement is positive but limited.
